title: The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
premise: A London lawyer grows alarmed by his old friend Dr. Jekyll's attachment to the repellent Edward Hyde, who has a key to the doctor's laboratory and stands to inherit his fortune. A brutal crime and Jekyll's increasing seclusion deepen a mystery guarded by friendship, professional honour and shame.
hook: A respectable doctor's back door opens onto a life his closest friends cannot imagine.
logline: As Hyde's violence threatens Dr. Jekyll's reputation and life, Utterson tries to protect his friend without knowing the secret that binds the two men.

world.setting: London, chiefly the respectable houses around Jekyll's square and Cavendish Square, a prosperous shopping by-street, Hyde's dismal Soho lodging, and the courts and rooms connecting them.
world.period: Victorian London, in an unspecified year of the 1800s
rules: Jekyll and Hyde are two bodily forms of one person, with memory in common; Jekyll is morally mixed, while he describes Hyde as wholly evil.
Jekyll's drug changes his body as well as his character. The same preparation restores him, but its action becomes uncertain and changes into Hyde begin without a dose.
The effective draught depends on an old salt supply; Jekyll believes an unknown impurity made it work, and fresh supplies fail to restore him.
Hyde is smaller and younger than Jekyll; clothes made for the doctor hang grotesquely loose on him. Witnesses sense deformity without identifying a specific malformation.
Respectable gentlemen guard reputations and confidences; a scandal or criminal association can ruin a name, while servants defer to their employers.
Letters travel by post or messenger; cabs and walking carry people through streets lit by gas lamps. Police investigate murder and circulate descriptions.

A will can transfer Jekyll's property on death or, under its unusual terms, prolonged disappearance; Utterson treats his clients' papers and a dead friend's sealed instructions as binding confidences.
world.tone: Sober, intimate and increasingly dreadful, with everyday comforts made uncanny by secrecy and sudden violence.
themes: The division and entanglement of good and evil
sensitivities: The narrative associates perceived ugliness, small stature and unspecified deformity with moral evil; those associations reflect its period rather than a reliable judgment of real bodies.
Hyde's violence against a child, a woman and Carew is described through intense horror; Carew's beating is especially graphic.
Class prejudice colours descriptions of Soho, its residents and servants, including references to women's nationalities.

voice.narration: A past-tense third-person narrator follows Utterson closely through the mystery, reporting his conjectures without granting him the hidden truth. The final two chapters change to Lanyon's and Jekyll's first-person written testimony, each with his own judgment and limits.
style: Long, balanced sentences accumulate clauses and qualifications, then yield to a short exclamation or sentence of dread.
Formal moral and legal diction mingles with vivid bodily sensations: cold blood, sickened flesh, trembling and a weight on the mind.
Fog, lamplight, doors and firelight make familiar London streets and rooms alternately welcoming and sinister.
The narrator describes outward gestures and rooms precisely, then moves into a character's doubts, often marking a supposition as such.
Colons, semicolons and dashes support elaborate turns of thought; pointed repetitions make fear and insistence audible.
British forms and period vocabulary include 'storey', 'neighbourhood', 'chemist', 'cab' and 'hansom'.
Jekyll's confession shifts between analytical argument, religious imagery and impassioned self-accusation, sometimes calling Hyde 'he'.
voice.dialogue: Double quotation marks frame spoken exchanges; quoted speech within a story uses single marks. Gentlemen address one another by surname and use courteous circumlocution, while fear breaks through in repetitions, abrupt questions and appeals to God. Servants say 'sir' but speak plainly and insistently when pressed.
samplePassages: Two doors from one corner, on the left hand going east the line was broken by the entry of a court; and just at that point a certain sinister block of building thrust forward its gable on the street. It was two storeys high; showed no window, nothing but a door on the lower storey and a blind forehead of discoloured wall on the upper; and bore in every feature, the marks of prolonged and sordid negligence. The door, which was equipped with neither bell nor knocker, was blistered and distained.

The besiegers, appalled by their own riot and the stillness that had succeeded, stood back a little and peered in. There lay the cabinet before their eyes in the quiet lamplight, a good fire glowing and chattering on the hearth, the kettle singing its thin strain, a drawer or two open, papers neatly set forth on the business table, and nearer the fire, the things laid out for tea; the quietest room, you would have said, and, but for the glazed presses full of chemicals, the most commonplace that night in London.

The most racking pangs succeeded: a grinding in the bones, deadly nausea, and a horror of the spirit that cannot be exceeded at the hour of birth or death. Then these agonies began swiftly to subside, and I came to myself as if out of a great sickness. There was something strange in my sensations, something indescribably new and, from its very novelty, incredibly sweet. I felt younger, lighter, happier in body; within I was conscious of a heady recklessness, a current of disordered sensual images running like a millrace in my fancy, a solution of the bonds of obligation, an unknown but not an innocent freedom of the soul.

cast.name: Mr. Utterson
cast.role: Lawyer, Jekyll's old friend and the chief investigator of the mystery.
cast.appearance: Lean and long, with a rugged, unsmiling face and sober, dusty appearance. He wears a dark Victorian suit, collar and tie, with a greatcoat and hat outdoors; his posture is reserved and upright. His hair is short and dark with some grey, his complexion pale and his eyes grey.
cast.personality: Austere, loyal and undemonstrative; his tolerance appears in practical help and in the discretion he grants troubled friends.
cast.motivation: He wants to protect Jekyll from disgrace and danger while honouring his duties as lawyer, trustee and friend.
cast.fears: He fears Hyde may ruin or murder Jekyll, and that a friend's hidden disgrace may come to light.
cast.speech: His speech is spare, courteous and probing, with 'Tut-tut' and carefully framed questions. With friends he can be dryly playful; under pressure he becomes firm and direct.
cast.arc: A reluctant investigator who prizes privacy, he moves from suspicion of blackmail to forcing the cabinet door, then reads the testimony that exposes the truth.

relationships.nature: Old friend and client whose safety and reputation he tries to protect.
Distrusted beneficiary of Jekyll's will whom he suspects of threatening the doctor.
Old school and college friend and fellow friend of Jekyll.
Distant kinsman and regular Sunday walking companion.
Jekyll's trusted servant, with whom he forces the cabinet.

cast.name: Mr. Enfield
cast.role: Man about town whose account of Hyde first alarms Utterson.
cast.appearance: A young, well-dressed Victorian gentleman of medium height and build, with a clean-shaven face, short brown hair, fair skin and brown eyes. He carries a cane and wears a dark coat, waistcoat, trousers and hat, standing erect on his walks.
cast.personality: Sociable, observant and decisive in an emergency, but ordinarily reluctant to ask questions that may expose a scandal.
cast.motivation: He wants the trampled child's family compensated and values discretion and his regular walks with Utterson.
cast.fears: He recoils from Hyde and dislikes the unpredictable harm caused by prying into private affairs.
cast.speech: He tells a fluent, colloquial story full of vivid comparisons and asides: 'Well, sir' and 'my gentleman'. He becomes terse and solemn when truly shocked.
cast.arc: His story sets the investigation in motion; later he discovers the door leads to Jekyll's and witnesses the doctor's terrifying change of expression.

relationships.nature: Distant cousin and devoted companion on Sunday walks.
Caught him after he trampled a child and extracted compensation.
Meets him at the cabinet window through Utterson.

cast.name: Mr. Hyde
cast.role: Jekyll's younger, violent second form and Carew's murderer.
cast.appearance: Small, dwarfish and pale, with a disturbing face, displeasing smile and an impression of deformity that observers cannot locate. His hand is lean, corded, knuckly and darkly hairy. He moves lightly and swiftly; he usually dresses plainly, though Jekyll's rich sober clothes hang vastly too large on him. His dark hair is short and his eyes dark.
cast.personality: Self-centred, cruel and quick to rage, yet capable of cool calculation, fear and desperate self-preservation.
cast.motivation: He pursues unrestrained pleasure and power, then struggles to escape capture and keep himself alive.
cast.fears: He fears the gallows, death and Jekyll's power to end their shared life by suicide.
cast.speech: His voice is husky, whispering and somewhat broken. He can be sneeringly polite, but snaps, snarls and repeats urgent questions; before Lanyon he turns taunting and grandly theatrical.
cast.arc: A secret means of indulgence, he grows more powerful and violent, becomes a hunted murderer and finally kills himself when the cabinet is forced.

relationships.nature: His other form; they share memories and a life but come to hate each other.
Jekyll's lawyer, whom he meets at the laboratory door.
The passer-by who catches him after he tramples a child.
Jekyll's old colleague, before whom he changes back into Jekyll.
Jekyll's butler, who knows his appearance and suspects him of murder.

cast.name: Dr. Lanyon
cast.role: Established physician and Jekyll's estranged scientific colleague.
cast.age: An ageing physician, an old schoolmate of Jekyll and Utterson
cast.appearance: A hearty, healthy-looking, dapper gentleman with a red face and a shock of prematurely white hair. He is of medium height and solid build, with fair skin and blue-grey eyes, wearing a dark physician's coat, waistcoat and formal collar; he carries himself briskly.
cast.personality: Genial, decided and proud of his scientific standards, with genuine affection beneath a somewhat theatrical manner.
cast.motivation: He wants to uphold sound medicine and answer an old friend's desperate appeal, despite suspecting Jekyll is insane.
cast.fears: The transformation and Jekyll's revelations leave him terrified, sleepless and unable to bear further mention of him.
cast.speech: He speaks heartily and decisively, chuckles with friends and calls Jekyll's theories 'unscientific balderdash'. His written account is precise and professional until horror breaks through.
cast.arc: He helps retrieve Jekyll's chemicals, chooses to witness Hyde's transformation and dies after the shock, leaving a sealed narrative.

relationships.nature: Old school and college friend entrusted with his sealed account.
Former close friend whose scientific views estranged him.
The repellent visitor he sees transform into Jekyll.
Jekyll's butler assists him in opening the cabinet.

cast.name: Poole
cast.role: Jekyll's long-serving butler who summons Utterson when the cabinet becomes terrifying.
cast.appearance: An elderly, well-dressed butler of medium height and spare build, with a lined, clean-shaven face, short grey hair, fair skin and grey eyes. He wears a dark formal servant's coat and waistcoat with a white collar; he stands deferentially upright and carries a red pocket-handkerchief.
cast.personality: Respectful and loyal, but observant, resolute and capable of blunt insistence when he believes his master is in danger.
cast.motivation: He wants to find and protect the master he has served for twenty years and to end the fearful uncertainty in the house.
cast.fears: He believes Jekyll has been murdered and dreads the unknown figure shut in the cabinet.
cast.speech: He repeatedly addresses Utterson as 'sir', gives concrete evidence and uses homely emphases such as 'main angry' and 'my bible-word'. Terror makes him whisper or speak harshly.
cast.arc: Initially reassuring Utterson that Hyde has his master's authority, he comes to suspect foul play and helps break into the cabinet.

relationships.nature: His master of twenty years, whom he knows by voice, height and tread.
The trusted lawyer he calls for help and follows into the cabinet.
A man his master ordered the household to obey, later suspected of murder.
He receives the physician under Jekyll's written instructions.

cast.name: Dr. Jekyll
cast.role: Respected physician and experimenter whose divided life produces Hyde.
cast.age: Fifty when Utterson discusses the will with him
cast.appearance: A large, tall, well-made man with a smooth, handsome face, a slightly sly cast and large, firm, white hands. He wears a sober Victorian gentleman's suit and waistcoat. His hair is short and greying, his skin fair and his eyes grey; in his final illness he becomes visibly wasted and weak.
cast.personality: Affectionate and generous, but proud, secretive and susceptible to pleasure; his remorse coexists with a habit of excusing himself.
cast.motivation: He wants both public respect and freedom for concealed pleasures, then seeks to control Hyde and make amends for his harm.
cast.fears: He fears disgrace, permanent loss of his own identity and Hyde's violence; later he dreads sleep and the failure of his drug.
cast.speech: With friends he is warm and expansive, using repeated assurances and appeals to trust. Pressed about Hyde, he becomes pale, evasive and emphatic; his confession argues, qualifies and condemns itself.
cast.arc: He creates Hyde to separate his impulses, renounces him after murder, and struggles against involuntary change until the effective salt runs out.

relationships.nature: His own other form, first an instrument of freedom and finally a hated rival.
Beloved friend and lawyer whom he trusts but refuses to enlighten until his final papers.
Old friend estranged by scientific differences; his witness to the transformation.
His loyal butler, whom he sends in search of the old salt.
Utterson's cousin, briefly introduced at the cabinet window.

places.name: The by-street and laboratory door
places.description: A prosperous shopping street conceals the neglected back entrance to Jekyll's laboratory; Hyde uses its key.
places.visual: Freshly painted shop shutters and polished brass flank a court and a two-storey, windowless gable. Its blistered, stained door has neither bell nor knocker; children play on the steps and tramps strike matches on its panels.

places.name: Dr. Jekyll's house
places.description: Jekyll's comfortable front house stands in an old square, connected across a former garden to the laboratory.
places.visual: A wealthy front door with a fanlight opens onto a large, low hall paved with flags, warmed by an open fire and furnished with costly oak cabinets. A yard separates the house from the laboratory.

places.name: The laboratory and cabinet
places.description: A former surgeon's dissecting theatre, converted to chemical work, leads upstairs to Jekyll's private cabinet.
places.visual: A gaunt, windowless theatre holds chemical apparatus, crates and packing straw beneath a foggy cupola. Stairs rise to a red-baize door; beyond are glazed presses, a cheval-glass, a business table, a hearth and three dusty, iron-barred windows.

places.name: Hyde's house in Soho
places.description: Hyde's separate lodging lets him pursue his secret life away from Jekyll's respectable square.
places.visual: A dingy, muddy street has a gin palace, a low French eating house, ragged children and cheap shops. Inside, two rooms contain deep carpets, silver, elegant linen, wine and a good picture.

places.name: Dr. Lanyon's house
places.description: The physician's house in Cavendish Square is where Hyde brings Jekyll's desperate errand to its conclusion.
places.visual: A respectable London house with a pillared portico, dining-room and brightly lit consulting room. A drawer of powders, a phial and a notebook lies behind a consulting-room table.

places.name: Utterson's house and office
places.description: The lawyer's bachelor home shelters his fireside consultations and the safe containing confidential papers.
places.visual: A firelit room with a reading desk and old wine gives way to a private business room with a safe and candle; a great dark bed stands behind curtains.

timeline.title: Chapter 1: Story of the Door
timeline.summary: On a Sunday walk, Enfield tells Utterson how Hyde trampled a child and paid compensation with a respectable man's cheque. Utterson recognizes the unnamed connection, and the cousins agree not to discuss it again.
events: Utterson and Enfield pass a neglected door in a prosperous London by-street.
Enfield recounts catching a small man who calmly trampled a girl and bringing him back to her family.
Threatened with scandal, the man pays £10 in gold and a cheque for the balance of £100; the cheque proves genuine.
Enfield calls the place Black Mail House and explains his rule against asking intrusive questions.
Utterson asks the man's name and learns it is Hyde; Enfield confirms Hyde still has the door key.
Utterson admits he knows the cheque's drawer, and the cousins agree to let the matter rest.

knowledge.learns: Enfield's child-trampler is Hyde, who used and still possesses a key to the neglected door.
Utterson already knows the identity of the respectable man who signed the cheque.

timeline.title: Chapter 2: Search for Mr. Hyde
timeline.summary: Utterson studies Jekyll's will, consults Lanyon and seeks out Hyde. After meeting the repellent beneficiary, he learns that Jekyll's servants are ordered to obey him and fears for his friend.
events: Utterson rereads Jekyll's will, which leaves Hyde everything on death or an unexplained absence exceeding three months.
Lanyon says scientific differences have estranged him from Jekyll and that he has never heard of Hyde.
Haunted by imagined scenes of Hyde's cruelty, Utterson watches the laboratory door until Hyde appears.
Hyde shows his face, gives Utterson a Soho address and angrily denies that Jekyll described him.
At Jekyll's front house, Poole says the doctor is out and the household has orders to obey Hyde.
Utterson imagines an old disgrace binding Jekyll to Hyde and fears Hyde may want to hasten his inheritance.

knowledge.learns: Lanyon has never heard of Hyde and regards Jekyll's scientific ideas as unscientific.
Hyde has a Soho address, a key to the laboratory and authority over Jekyll's servants.
Utterson knows him by sight and is Jekyll's lawyer and old friend.

timeline.title: Chapter 3: Dr. Jekyll Was Quite at Ease
timeline.summary: After a dinner, Utterson urges Jekyll to confide in him about Hyde. Jekyll refuses, claims he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses and secures a promise that Utterson will protect Hyde's rights.
events: A fortnight later Utterson stays behind after one of Jekyll's dinners.
Jekyll dismisses Lanyon as a pedant and turns pale when Utterson mentions Hyde.
Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll calls the affair private and says he can be rid of Hyde at will.
Jekyll asks Utterson to bear with Hyde and secure his rights if Jekyll is taken away.
Despite admitting he cannot like Hyde, Utterson promises.

knowledge.learns: Utterson has heard something abominable about Hyde and remains willing to help Jekyll in confidence.
Jekyll claims he can end his connection with Hyde at will and asks that Hyde's rights be protected.

timeline.title: Chapter 4: The Carew Murder Case
timeline.summary: A maid witnesses Hyde beat Sir Danvers Carew to death. Utterson identifies the victim and the broken weapon, then leads Inspector Newcomen to Hyde's ransacked Soho rooms.
events: Nearly a year later, a maid sees Hyde attack an elderly gentleman with a cane in a moonlit lane.
The maid faints; on waking at two she summons police, who find a letter addressed to Utterson on the victim.
Utterson identifies the body as Sir Danvers Carew and recognizes the broken cane as one he gave Jekyll.
Utterson takes Inspector Newcomen by cab through fog to Hyde's Soho address.
Hyde's housekeeper admits the visitors; they find ransacked rooms, a burned cheque book and the other half of the cane.
The inspector finds money in Hyde's bank account and plans to watch for him, though witnesses cannot give a consistent description.

knowledge.learns: Hyde has been identified as Carew's killer, and the murder weapon was a cane Utterson gave Jekyll.
Hyde returned briefly to his Soho rooms after a long absence and left evidence there.

timeline.title: Chapter 5: Incident of the Letter
timeline.summary: Jekyll gives Utterson a letter supposedly from Hyde and swears he is finished with him. Poole's account and Guest's handwriting comparison leave the lawyer suspecting Jekyll forged it.
events: Poole leads Utterson through the former dissecting theatre to Jekyll's cabinet.
Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again and gives Utterson a letter in which Hyde claims a safe means of escape.
Jekyll says the letter was handed in and admits Hyde dictated the will's disappearance clause.
Poole tells Utterson no letter was delivered that day except posted circulars.
Over wine, Utterson shows the letter to his clerk Guest, who compares it with a new note from Jekyll.
Guest finds the hands nearly identical but differently sloped; Utterson locks up the note and suspects forgery.

knowledge.learns: Jekyll claims to have broken with Hyde and says Hyde proposed the will's disappearance clause.
Poole received no hand-delivered letter, and Guest finds a close resemblance between Hyde's and Jekyll's writing.
He comes to suspect that Jekyll forged a letter for the murderer.

timeline.title: Chapter 6: Incident of Dr. Lanyon
timeline.summary: Hyde remains missing while Jekyll enjoys a period of renewed friendship and good works. Abruptly Jekyll shuts himself away, Lanyon sickens and dies, and Utterson honours the seal on Lanyon's account.
events: Police uncover Hyde's disreputable past but cannot find him; Jekyll returns to society, charity and religion.
After dining with Jekyll and Lanyon on 8 January, Utterson is refused admission to Jekyll's house on subsequent visits.
Utterson finds Lanyon gravely changed; Lanyon says he has suffered a fatal shock and refuses to discuss Jekyll.
In a letter, Jekyll confirms an incurable breach with Lanyon and asks Utterson to respect his seclusion.
Lanyon dies, and Utterson opens an outer envelope addressed to him but leaves the inner narrative sealed as instructed.
Poole reports Jekyll's continued confinement to the cabinet, and Utterson gradually visits less often.

knowledge.learns: Lanyon regards Jekyll as dead to him and attributes his own decline to an unnamed shock.
Jekyll believes his estrangement from Lanyon is incurable and says he has brought an unnamed punishment and danger on himself.
Lanyon's inner account must remain sealed until Jekyll's death or disappearance.

timeline.mood: Brief renewal, then dread and bereavement

timeline.title: Chapter 7: Incident at the Window
timeline.summary: On their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield see Jekyll at his cabinet window. He refuses a walk, then abruptly shuts the window with a look of terror that leaves both men shaken.
events: Enfield tells Utterson he has discovered that the neglected door is a back entrance to Jekyll's house.
The cousins enter the court and find Jekyll sitting at the half-open middle window.
Jekyll says he is very low and refuses Utterson's invitation to walk, though he welcomes their company from below.
His smile abruptly gives way to terror and despair, and he thrusts down the window.
The two men leave in silence; Utterson says, 'God forgive us.'

knowledge.learns: Enfield has discovered the connection between the by-street door and Jekyll's house.
Utterson has met Hyde and shares his repulsion.
Jekyll says he cannot venture out and witnesses a sudden, terrifying change in his expression.
He witnesses Jekyll's sudden expression of terror and the abrupt closing of the window.

timeline.title: Chapter 8: The Last Night
timeline.summary: Poole brings Utterson to Jekyll's frightened household. They force the cabinet and find Hyde dead, Jekyll missing and papers directing Utterson to read Lanyon's narrative and Jekyll's confession.
events: On a wild March evening, Poole tells Utterson he fears foul play and takes him to the house.
Poole makes Utterson hear the changed voice behind the cabinet door and describes urgent, unsuccessful searches for a chemical.
Poole says he saw a masked, dwarf-sized figure; he and Utterson come to believe Hyde has murdered Jekyll.
They station Bradshaw and the boy at the back door, then force the cabinet after the voice begs for mercy.
They find Hyde dead in Jekyll's oversized clothes, a crushed phial in his hand, and search in vain for Jekyll.
A broken, rusty key lies by the locked laboratory door; in the cabinet they find a new will naming Utterson and a note dated that day.
Jekyll's note directs Utterson to Lanyon's narrative and his own sealed confession; Utterson takes the papers home, planning to return before calling police.

knowledge.learns: Poole believes the voice and masked figure are not Jekyll's and suspects Hyde; Utterson comes to share the murder theory.
The cabinet occupant repeatedly rejected fresh chemical supplies as impure and urgently sought an older sample.
Hyde is dead in the cabinet, apparently by his own hand, while Jekyll is nowhere found.
A new will names him beneficiary, and Jekyll's note dated that day anticipates his disappearance and directs him to the narratives.
The cabinet contains Hyde's body but no trace of Jekyll, and the laboratory-door key is broken and rusty.

timeline.title: Chapter 9: Dr. Lanyon’s Narrative
timeline.summary: Lanyon's written account reveals how he obeyed Jekyll's urgent letter, fetched a chemical drawer and watched the strange messenger drink a mixture and become Jekyll.
events: Lanyon receives Jekyll's registered appeal to retrieve a drawer from his cabinet and give it to a midnight messenger.
With Poole and tradesmen, Lanyon opens the cabinet, takes the specified drawer and examines its powders, red liquor and record book.
Expecting a madman's errand, Lanyon loads a revolver and admits a small, oddly dressed stranger at midnight.
The stranger mixes the powder and liquor, then offers Lanyon a choice between letting him leave and witnessing a revelation.
Lanyon chooses to see; the visitor drinks and transforms into Jekyll.
Jekyll tells Lanyon more; Lanyon records his horror and identifies the visitor as Hyde, Carew's murderer.

knowledge.learns: Jekyll urgently needs the contents of a specified drawer delivered to a messenger, though Lanyon initially believes him insane.
The visitor transforms before his eyes into Jekyll and, by Jekyll's confession, is Hyde, the wanted murderer.
By reading Lanyon's narrative, he learns that Hyde and Jekyll are the same person and that Lanyon witnessed the transformation.

timeline.title: Chapter 10: Henry Jekyll’s Full Statement of the Case
timeline.summary: Jekyll's confession traces his concealed pleasures, the discovery of the transforming drug, Hyde's crimes and the collapse of his control. Unable to replace the effective salt, he seals his account before his final change.
events: Jekyll describes his divided ambitions and the first draught that makes him Hyde; a second restores his original form.
He establishes Hyde's lodging, authority and inheritance, and uses the disguise for secret pleasures that grow cruel.
After waking involuntarily as Hyde, he chooses to live as Jekyll, but drinks again after two months.
Hyde murders Carew; Jekyll returns in remorse, locks the laboratory door and crushes its key.
After a period of good works, Jekyll changes involuntarily in Regent's Park and, as Hyde, sends Lanyon and Poole registered instructions.
Restored at Lanyon's, Jekyll soon suffers repeated involuntary changes, needing increasingly frequent doses and dreading sleep.
Fresh salt fails; believing the original supply contained a necessary impurity, Jekyll finishes and seals his confession under the last effective dose.

knowledge.learns: His first experiment produces a smaller form expressing his lower nature, and the draught can restore his original body.
An involuntary change during sleep reveals that he is losing control of Hyde; he chooses abstinence but later breaks it.
After Carew's murder he learns the crime was witnessed and Hyde is publicly identified and hunted.
An involuntary change in Regent's Park leaves him unable to reach his drugs safely, so he devises the appeal to Lanyon.
Fresh salt fails, and he comes to believe an unknown impurity in the original supply was essential.
The confession explains Jekyll's experiments, Hyde's crimes, the involuntary changes and the exhaustion of the effective salt.

divergencePoints.label: The Cheque Is Refused
divergencePoints.moment: After Hyde tramples the child, Enfield and the others threaten scandal and demand compensation.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Hyde produces gold and Jekyll's cheque; the party waits for the bank and finds the cheque genuine.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Enfield refused Hyde's money and took him to the police over the trampled child?
divergencePoints.stakes: The child's family's compensation and Jekyll's concealed connection to Hyde are at stake.

divergencePoints.label: A Clean Breast
divergencePoints.moment: Utterson offers Jekyll confidential help and asks him to make a clean breast of his trouble with Hyde.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Jekyll thanks him but refuses to explain, insists he can be rid of Hyde and asks him to protect Hyde's rights.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Jekyll told Utterson the truth about Hyde by the fireside after dinner?
divergencePoints.stakes: Jekyll risks his reputation and the friendship on which he most relies.

divergencePoints.label: The Cane Held Back
divergencePoints.moment: Carew politely addresses Hyde in the moonlit lane while Hyde grips a heavy cane and struggles with impatience.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Hyde flies into a rage and beats Carew to death, breaking the cane.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Hyde mastered his rage and let Sir Danvers Carew walk away from their meeting?
divergencePoints.stakes: Carew's life and the exposure of Hyde's violence hang on the encounter.

divergencePoints.label: The Seal Broken
divergencePoints.moment: After Lanyon's funeral, Utterson holds the inner narrative marked for opening only after Jekyll's death or disappearance.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Professional honour and loyalty prevail over curiosity, and he locks the sealed packet away.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Utterson broke Lanyon's seal and read the narrative immediately after the funeral?
divergencePoints.stakes: The truth becomes available at the cost of a dead friend's explicit confidence.

divergencePoints.label: At The Window
divergencePoints.moment: Jekyll tells Utterson and Enfield he cannot go out but is glad to see them at his open window.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: He agrees to talk from above, then suddenly looks terrified and shuts the window.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Jekyll invited Utterson and Enfield up to the cabinet when they found him at the window?
divergencePoints.stakes: A desperate man might gain company while exposing the secret he is struggling to conceal.

divergencePoints.label: Hyde Begs For Mercy
divergencePoints.moment: As Utterson demands entry to the cabinet, the voice inside begs him for mercy.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Recognizing Hyde's voice, Utterson orders Poole to strike the door; they find Hyde dead.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Utterson answered Hyde's plea and tried to draw him out before Poole struck the door?
divergencePoints.stakes: Hyde's life and any chance of learning Jekyll's whereabouts depend on the exchange.

divergencePoints.label: Lanyon's Choice
divergencePoints.moment: With the prepared glass in hand, Hyde offers Lanyon the choice of letting him leave or witnessing a revelation.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Lanyon chooses to see the end and watches Hyde transform into Jekyll.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Lanyon let the stranger take the glass and leave without witnessing the transformation?
divergencePoints.stakes: Lanyon's understanding of his old friend and his exposure to a devastating shock are at stake.

divergencePoints.label: The First Draught
divergencePoints.moment: Jekyll has prepared the transforming mixture and hesitates over the risk of death before testing it on himself.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Temptation overcomes his fear; he drinks and becomes Hyde for the first time.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Jekyll put down the glass and refused to drink the first transforming draught?
divergencePoints.stakes: His discovery and the possibility of giving his hidden impulses a separate body remain unresolved.

divergencePoints.label: The Missing Salt
divergencePoints.moment: Jekyll's original salt runs low and fresh supplies fail to make an effective draught.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: The search across London fails, and Jekyll concludes that an unknown impurity in the old supply was essential.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Poole found a remaining quantity of the old salt among the chemists' supplies?
divergencePoints.stakes: Jekyll's access to his own form and the length of his struggle with Hyde depend on the supply.

visual.era: Victorian London: dark frock coats, waistcoats, long dresses and servant livery; gas lamps, hansom cabs, masonry terraces and chemical glassware.
visual.palette: Coal black, fog brown and grey against warm firelight, brass and the red of baize and chemical tincture; cold moonlight for the murder.
motifs: A blistered door and its key
visual.comicStyle: Victorian engraved-book illustration in ink, with fine cross-hatching, dense shadow and restrained colour washes. Use measured panels for formal rooms and conversations, tightening into close views of hands, faces, locks and glass when dread interrupts ordinary life.

glossary.note: Respectable physician and experimenter Henry Jekyll.
Edward Hyde, Jekyll's smaller and violent second form.
Gabriel John Utterson, lawyer and old friend of Jekyll.
Richard Enfield, Utterson's kinsman and walking companion.
Hastie Lanyon, physician and witness to the transformation.
An elderly member of Parliament murdered by Hyde.
The Scotland Yard inspector investigating Carew's murder.
Utterson's head clerk and student of handwriting.
Enfield's name for the building with the neglected door.
The medical district where Lanyon lives and receives patients.
The district containing Hyde's separate lodging.
Jekyll's private room above the laboratory theatre.
The standing mirror Jekyll keeps in his cabinet to observe transformations.
A firm asked to search for Jekyll's old chemical supply.
A hired carriage used for journeys through London.
